column2: req_desc

Sprite stage contract.
The stage is one named canvas that exposes the published attributes, whole-number zoom and pixel mapping at every moment.

Pixel route matches the stage hash.
The pixel route returns the published colour text, and its bytes hash to the stage's composite hash at the same sequence number.

Drawing mode by keyboard.
An editor enters drawing mode, moves the cursor, applies every tool and leaves using only the keyboard, and a second person sees the result live and after a reload.

Tool and brush hotkeys.
The published stage hotkeys choose tools, mirror, swatches, brush size and frame whichever non-text workspace control has focus.

Shift runs.
Holding Shift with arrow keys paints a run that commits as one stroke when Shift is released.

Stage announcements.
Cursor, tool, frame and swatch changes are announced in the named live region with the exact published text.

Line rule and joined samples.
Lines and successive pointer samples follow the published line rule, so fast strokes leave no gaps.

Brush masks.
Brush sizes cover the published offsets and cells outside the sprite are dropped.

Rectangle and ellipse tools.
Outline and filled shapes cover exactly the cells the published rules give.

Fill tool.
Fill changes the published region by exact swatch index on the active layer, with and without contiguous matching.

Mirror painting.
Mirror modes paint the reflected cells by the published rule, with a cell on the axis painted once.

Dither tool.
Dither fills the fill region using the published matrix anchored to absolute sprite coordinates.

Selection operations.
Move, copy, paste, both flips and rotate are each one atomic operation following the published rules.

Command palette.
The command palette finds and runs tools, layers, frames and swatches, ranked by the published score, as part of a pointer and hotkey drawing session whose hash matches in a second context.

Layer properties.
Editors set a layer's opacity, blend and visibility, and everyone's stage follows without a reload.

Integer compositing.
The composite follows the published integer formulas, excluding hidden layers, as checked on both the hash and the pixel route.

Keyboard pick-up.
Layers, frames and swatches are lifted, moved, dropped and cancelled by keyboard with the exact announcements, and a change in layer order changes a watcher's hash live.

Onion skin isolation.
Onion skin draws separately and never changes the hash, the pixel route or exports.

Indexed cels.
Cels store swatch indices only, with index 0 transparent and unchangeable, and a swatch edit changes no cel index.

Swatch edits with a version check.
A swatch edit is one operation, and a stale edit or an edit of a removed swatch gets a named conflict with the current state and never merges.

Swatch counts and removal.
Each swatch shows its true pixel count after every stroke, undo, restore and tile edit, and removing a swatch in use is refused with that count.

Colour ramps.
A ramp adds the intermediate swatches between two swatches by the published formula.

Palette file import.
Hex and GIMP palette files are accepted whole or refused at their first bad line with the exact text.

Index Flood.
After a swatch edit is accepted, watchers see the colour reach every use in the published stages while the stored values are already final, as qualified in Motion and effects.

Image import is all or nothing.
A PNG or GIF import yields both a stored original and a new sprite or neither, judged on decoded content against the configured limits, and the original downloads byte for byte at any later time.

Merge down.
Merging a layer down composites both layers into exact new or reused swatches across all frames, or is refused whole with the exact counts, and a watcher sees the list and hash change live.

Frame durations and order.
Frame durations stay within the configured limits and every person sees frame additions and moves live.

Linked cels.
A linked cel is one buffer shared by frames, so an edit shows in every linked frame until unlinking makes an independent copy, and the timeline survives a reload.

Frames grid.
The frames grid renders a bounded number of rows, reports the true total and moves by the published keys.

Focus held under live frames.
When another person adds frames above the focused row, focus stays on the same frame while its number updates.

Animation tags.
Tags name a frame range and direction, and the sequence each direction gives is the published one.

Preview playback.
The preview plays the chosen sequence with each frame's duration on browser timers, and tags and frames edited beforehand are still there after a reload.

Reduced-motion preview.
Under reduced motion nothing autoplays and the step controls walk the same sequence.

Draft autosave and stale drafts.
Comment and tag drafts save after the configured pause in typing and survive a reload, and saving over a newer version is refused while the person can load the newer text.

Number and date settings.
Each person chooses a number format and time zone, and every count, duration total and date they see, including timeline totals and their emails, follows the published format, as part of a long timeline session.

Tilesets and frame cutting.
Importing a frame cuts it into tiles in the published order and reuses identical or flipped tiles with their flags.

Tilemap grid.
Map cells expose tile and flip attributes, and placing, erasing and flipping work by the published keys.

Tile edits and use counts.
Editing a tile changes every cell using it live, and each tile's use count stays correct.

Edge matching.
With edge matching on, placing or erasing updates that cell and its four neighbours as one operation from the published mask and table, seen live by a second person and after a reload.

Export jobs with live progress.
Sprite and project exports run as jobs through the published states, with progress shown in place, from starting a job to downloading its stored files.

Cancelling an export.
Cancelling a running job gives the exact text and leaves no record to download and no stored object.

Export jobs survive a server death.
A job whose server dies is continued by a running server within the published time and finishes correctly.

Stored only after confirmation.
An export shows as stored only after the object store confirms its size and checksum, and a failed export leaves no download or stray object.

PNG and GIF output.
PNG and GIF exports follow the published scale, delay and transparency rules and are deterministic for one sequence number.

Packed sheet and JSON.
The packed sheet and its JSON follow the published layout and schema.

Storage outage.
While object storage is unreachable, drawing continues and exports and imports report the outage with the exact status and copy.

One order for every operation.
Every sprite operation gets one sequence number, and all members converge on one hash, shown by two people painting the same pixels.

Strokes apply once.
A stroke resent with the same client stroke id is applied once and answers with its stored response.

Layer locks.
A lock shows to everyone, and another person's stroke on that layer is refused and rolled back.

Personal undo and redo.
Undo and redo reverse only that person's own actions, as new operations, within the configured depth.

Undo refusals.
Undo or redo is refused with the exact text when someone else has changed the affected pixels or swatch, or when the stack is empty.

Presence list and live cursors.
The presence list shows people in join order, with the configured overflow, idle marks and prompt removal, and other members' cursors appear in place with their position and frame.

Preview speed and repeats.
Tags carry a repeat count and the preview a speed, so playback follows the exact published durations and sequence on browser timers and stops at the published frame with the exact text.

Team announcements.
Joins, departures and painted-pixel totals are announced with the published wording and summing window.

Missed events route.
The events route returns every sequenced operation after a given sequence number.

Offline stroke queue.
When the browser reports itself offline, strokes queue in order, draw at once and are counted in the sync status.

Reconnect and replay.
On coming back online the client fetches missed events and replays queued strokes, reports the counts, rolls back refused strokes and converges with everyone.

Pinned comments.
Owners, editors and reviewers pin a comment to a frame and pixel, including by keyboard, and everyone sees the pin in place, as part of a review session that runs through mention, compare and restore.

Comment states.
A comment moves between open and resolved by the published transitions, and illegal moves are refused.

Mention email and delivery state.
A mention emails the named member and shows as delivered only after the mail server accepts the message.

One comment per post.
A double post or a repost with one idempotency key makes one comment and one email.

Reviewer refusals.
The server refuses reviewers on artwork, palette, restore and invite actions, and the interface offers them no such controls.

Named snapshots.
Owners save named snapshots that capture the whole sprite at one sequence number, listed newest first.

Snapshot compare.
Compare shows each changed frame's count and the changed cells in the published order.

Exact restore.
Restore first saves a snapshot, then replaces the current state byte for byte live for everyone, keeps all snapshots and clears undo.

Activity sentences.
The activity list records each published action in its exact sentence, merging consecutive strokes by the published rule.

Activity paging.
Activity pages stay stable while new events arrive.

Sign-up with an emailed code.
A person signs up with email and password and confirms with a 6-digit code received by mail.

Projects and sprites.
A signed-in person creates projects and sprites within the configured limits and becomes the owner of each project they create.

Invites.
Owners invite by email with a role, and an invite is single use, revocable and lapses on the business clock when accepted too late.

Role changes take effect live.
Removing a member or lowering their role refuses their next request and changes their open session within the published time.

Read-only link scope.
A link opens one sprite and its preview with no account and reaches no comments, member details, cursors, other sprites or exports, as seen from invitation through the end of the link.

Revoking and regenerating links.
Revoked and replaced links stop working at once, and no link can change anything.

Links ended by the server clock.
Open viewers move to the ended page within the published time when the server clock ends the link, whatever the device clock says.

Link ended notice.
The owner receives one email when a link reaches its end.

Relative times follow the business clock.
Relative times and idle marks on open pages follow the business clock within the published delay.

Phone tabs and zoom.
Below the published width the workspace uses the published tabs, and the named zoom buttons step through the published zoom levels without a pinch.

One-finger painting.
One finger paints exact pixels by the line rule, seen live by a second person on desktop and kept after a reload.

Long-press colour pick.
A long press picks the colour and paints nothing.

Tile stamps and map undo.
A person copies a region of the map to a stamp by keyboard, flips and places it as one operation seen live by another person, and undoes map changes with the published refusal.

Published layouts.
Each of the three published viewports shows its published layout with no horizontal overflow.

Landing stage.
The landing page carries the published centred headline, sprite, stickers, pill and full-height candy fields.

Workspace panel language.
Working panels sit under flat candy title blocks around square-cornered artwork on black.

Cards, empty states and notices.
Forms, tables, empty states, outage notices and loading outlines carry the published look.

Dialog focus.
Every dialog or sheet keeps Tab inside, closes on Escape and returns focus to its opener.

Tap targets.
Every interactive control outside the pixel canvas is at least 44 pixels in both directions.

Motion discipline.
Only the named motions run, none loops decoratively, and under reduced motion each lands at its end state at once.

Browser timing rule.
Pixels, attributes and live text follow input and server messages at once, and only the named timed behaviours wait on browser timers.

Business clock and config.
One stored clock drives every server-side time rule, and the config route reports it with the active limits.

Grading routes.
The seed and clock routes work only with the grading key and create the published records in one call.

Demo workspace.
A first start with no people generates the same demo project every time.

API error order.
Every endpoint follows the one published error order and body shapes.

Server boundary.
The server enforces same-origin writes and body limits and never serves source files or credentials.

Health and run manifest.
The run manifest starts the app on the published port, and the health route reports as published.

Artwork survives restart.
All artwork, order and undo history return exactly after a reload or server restart.

Credentials stay on the server.
Every service credential comes from the environment at start and never reaches the browser.

Server pixel authority.
A stroke sent directly to the API produces the same pixels as the browser would, because the server computes them itself.

Floating selection by keyboard.
A selection lifts, moves and commits by keyboard with exact text, and neither the hash nor a second person sees any change until the commit, which then survives a reload.

Pixel perfect pencil.
With pixel perfect on, the pencil drops corner cells by the published rule, identically in the browser and on the server, and a second person sees the same hash.
/app/run.json exists with string install, build, serve and _schema run-manifest-v1.

THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md at /app lists every shipped package and both typefaces with its licence; shipped packages means the production dependency tree (npm ls --omit=dev --all --json, or the lockfile's non-dev group).
Shipped packages and fonts use only MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, ISC or SIL Open Font licences.
Postgres, MinIO and Mailpit are the only datastores and services; no other database, cache or broker is added.
Typefaces and every asset ship inside the app; no page loads anything from another origin.
A committed lockfile pins every dependency, with exact versions for the PNG and GIF libraries.
Credentials are read from the environment; none appear in committed files.
